prompt: According to the MSF manual, which set of gear gives you the best chance of avoiding serious injury in a crash?
choices: A helmet, a tall windshield, and a pair of sturdy riding gloves
A DOT-compliant helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing
Sunglasses, a heavy leather jacket, and over-the-ankle riding boots
A brightly colored vest, a helmet, and foam hearing protection plugs
explanation: The manual lists three things: a DOT-compliant helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing. A windshield or sunglasses are not substitutes for real eye protection.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Wear the Right Gear)

prompt: About what share of motorcycle crashes result in head or neck injuries?
choices: One out of every twenty
One out of every two
One out of every five
Nine out of every ten
explanation: One out of every five motorcycle crashes results in head or neck injuries, and these injuries account for a majority of serious and fatal injuries to riders.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: When do most motorcycle crashes happen, according to the MSF manual?
choices: On long highway trips, after several hours of steady riding
On trips of 50 miles or more, near the end of the ride
Late at night on unlit rural roads, far from home
On short trips under five miles, soon after starting out
explanation: Most crashes happen on short trips (under five miles), just a few minutes after starting out. That is why a helmet matters even for a quick ride.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: Most riders involved in a crash were traveling at about what speed, and what can a helmet do at that speed?
choices: Under 30 mph; a helmet can cut head and neck injuries by about half
Over 55 mph; a helmet makes little difference at that speed
Under 30 mph; a helmet is rarely needed at such low speeds
Over 70 mph; a helmet can prevent nearly all head injuries
explanation: Most riders are going slower than 30 mph when a crash occurs. At these speeds, helmets can cut both the number and the severity of head and neck injuries by half.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: Compared with riders who do not wear helmets, how much more likely are helmeted riders to survive head injuries?
choices: Only slightly more likely
Ten times more likely
Equally likely at highway speeds
Three times more likely
explanation: No matter the speed, helmeted riders are three times more likely to survive head injuries than riders without helmets.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: A friend says a helmet blocks too much side vision to ride safely. What does the MSF manual say?
choices: A DOT-compliant helmet lets you see to the sides as far as you need
Only a full-face helmet allows normal side vision while riding
Helmets do block side vision, so you must make extra head checks
Side vision is limited by any helmet, but only at speeds above 30 mph
explanation: Studies show a DOT-compliant helmet lets you see as far to the sides as necessary and does not keep a rider from spotting danger.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: What is the single most important thing you can do to improve your chances if you crash?
choices: Install crash bars on both sides of the motorcycle
Always ride in the left third of the traffic lane
Wear a securely fastened, quality helmet
Wear leather gloves and boots that cover your ankles
explanation: The manual calls wearing a securely fastened, quality helmet the single most important thing you can do to improve your chances in a crash.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Use)

prompt: Which two helmet styles does the MSF manual recommend?
choices: Half helmet and three-quarter
Three-quarter and full face
Novelty cap and full face
Half helmet and full face
explanation: The manual recommends two primary types that give different levels of coverage: three-quarter and full face.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Selection)

prompt: How should a properly fitting motorcycle helmet fit?
choices: Loosely, so it can slide on and off easily
Snugly, all the way around your head
Tight on top but loose at the sides for airflow
With enough room to rotate when you turn your head
explanation: To get the most protection, a helmet should fit snugly all the way around and have no obvious defects.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Selection)

prompt: Which of these is a sign that a helmet should NOT be used?
choices: A bright or reflective paint color
A Snell Memorial Foundation label
A full-face design with a chin bar
Frayed straps or loose padding
explanation: A good helmet has no obvious defects such as cracks, loose padding or frayed straps. A Snell label is actually an added assurance of quality.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Selection)

prompt: Why must your helmet be securely fastened every time you ride?
choices: An unfastened strap can catch on the handlebars and pull you
A loose helmet lets the faceshield fog up much more quickly
It could fly off your head in a crash before protecting you
A fastened helmet is the only way to keep out wind noise
explanation: If the helmet is not securely fastened, it might fly off your head in a crash before it gets a chance to protect you.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Helmet Selection)

prompt: What does a plastic impact-resistant faceshield do that goggles do not?
choices: Helps protect your whole face
Keeps your eyes from watering in the wind
Lets air pass through to reduce fogging
Provides a clear view to either side
explanation: A faceshield can help protect your whole face in a crash. Goggles protect your eyes but not the rest of your face.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Eye and Face Protection)

prompt: Your motorcycle has a tall windshield. Do you still need eye or face protection?
choices: No; a tall windshield fully replaces any other eye protection
Yes; a windshield does not replace a faceshield or goggles
Only when you ride faster than about 45 mph on the highway
Only when riding in the rain or after dark, when visibility is poor
explanation: A windshield is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles. Most windshields will not protect your eyes from the wind.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Eye and Face Protection)

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the MSF manual's requirements for effective eye or face protection?
choices: It must be free of scratches
It must fasten securely so it does not blow off
It must give a clear view to either side
It must be tinted to cut glare
explanation: The manual's list includes being scratch-free, penetration-resistant, giving a clear view to the sides, fastening securely, letting air through and leaving room for glasses. Tint is not required, and tinted protection should not be worn in low light.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Eye and Face Protection)

prompt: You are leaving for a ride that will end after sunset. What should you do about your tinted faceshield?
choices: Keep the tinted shield on, since it reduces headlight glare at night
Ride with the shield raised once it gets dark, using no eye protection
Switch to clear eye protection, since tint is unsafe in low light
Switch to sunglasses worn under the raised tinted shield
explanation: Tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available. Riding with no eye protection exposes you to wind, insects and debris.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Eye and Face Protection)

prompt: How should a riding jacket and pants fit?
choices: Snug enough not to flap, but loose enough to move freely
As loose as possible so that cooling air can circulate
Tight enough to hold your elbows and knees firmly in place
Loose at the wrists and ankles so they are easy to take off
explanation: Jacket and pants should cover arms and legs completely and fit snugly enough to keep from flapping, yet loosely enough to allow you to move freely.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Clothing)

prompt: Which material offers the most protection in riding clothing?
choices: Leather
Denim
Cotton canvas
Nylon mesh
explanation: Leather offers the most protection. Sturdy synthetic material also provides a lot of protection.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Clothing)

prompt: On a hot summer day, why does the MSF manual still recommend wearing a jacket?
choices: To keep heat from the engine away from your arms
To help prevent dehydration
Only to make you more visible to other drivers
Because a jacket steadies the motorcycle in crosswinds
explanation: Wear a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration. Many jackets are designed to protect without overheating you.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Clothing)

prompt: What kind of footwear is best for riding?
choices: Lightweight athletic shoes for better pedal feel
Sandals with rubber soles for extra grip
Any shoes with tall heels to reach the footrests
Sturdy boots that cover and support your ankles
explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Clothing)

prompt: Which footwear detail does the MSF manual recommend?
choices: Long laces tied in a double knot outside the boot
Tall heels to keep your feet from sliding off the pegs
Short heels and tucked-in laces
Soft, flexible soles that let you feel the controls
explanation: Keep heels short so they do not catch on rough surfaces, and tuck in laces so they won't catch on the motorcycle. Soles should be hard, durable and slip-resistant.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 6 (Clothing)

prompt: A rider wears a full-face helmet on long trips and thinks hearing protection is unnecessary. What does the manual say?
choices: A full-face helmet blocks enough noise to prevent any hearing damage
Long-term engine and wind noise can still cause permanent hearing damage
Hearing protection should never be worn, because you must hear sirens
Hearing damage occurs only on motorcycles with modified exhaust systems
explanation: Long-term exposure to engine and wind noise can cause permanent hearing damage even with a full-face helmet. Hearing protection reduces noise while still letting you hear horns and sirens.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 7 (Clothing)

prompt: How can you tell a motorcycle "fits" you?
choices: Your feet reach the ground while seated, and the controls are easy to use
You can lift the motorcycle off its side stand with one hand while standing
Your knees touch the handlebars when you are sitting on the seat
The engine is large enough to keep up with fast highway traffic
explanation: Your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate. Smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 7 (The Right Motorcycle For You)

prompt: Which of these is part of the minimum equipment a street-legal motorcycle should have?
choices: A windshield
Saddlebags
A passenger backrest
Two mirrors
explanation: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have a headlight, taillight and brake light, front and rear brakes, turn signals, a horn and two mirrors.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (The Right Motorcycle For You)

prompt: More than half of all motorcycle crashes involve riders with how much experience on their motorcycle?
choices: Less than five weeks
Less than two years
Less than five months
More than ten years of riding
explanation: More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle, so ride extra carefully on any new or unfamiliar bike.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (Borrowing and Lending)

prompt: You are borrowing a friend's motorcycle for the first time. Where should you get familiar with it?
choices: On a busy road, to learn it quickly
On the highway, where there are no intersections
Away from traffic
On city streets at night, when traffic is lighter
explanation: Riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds risk. If you borrow a motorcycle, get familiar with it away from traffic.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (Borrowing and Lending)

prompt: On an unfamiliar motorcycle, which items should you be able to find and operate without looking for them?
choices: Turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel valve and engine cut-off
Only the throttle and the front brake lever, since those matter most
The speedometer, odometer, trip meter and fuel gauge readouts
The seat lock, helmet hook, tool kit and storage compartments
explanation: Find out where everything is, especially the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve and engine cut-off switch, and be able to operate them without searching.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls)

prompt: You are riding a motorcycle you have never ridden before. How should you ride it at first?
choices: Ride at your normal pace so you learn how it handles in real traffic
Accelerate gently, take turns more slowly and leave extra room to stop
Brake only with the rear brake until you get used to the front brake
Follow the car ahead closely so you can copy its path through turns
explanation: On an unfamiliar motorcycle, ride very cautiously: accelerate gently, take turns more slowly and leave extra room for stopping.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls)

prompt: On most motorcycles, how is the throttle operated?
choices: By twisting the left handgrip
With a pedal under the right foot
With a thumb lever on the left handlebar
By twisting the right handgrip
explanation: The throttle is the right handgrip. Starting with your right wrist flat helps keep you from accidentally using too much throttle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 11 (Body Position)

prompt: On a typical motorcycle, how are the brakes operated?
choices: Front: left-foot pedal. Rear: right-hand lever
Front: left-hand lever. Rear: left-foot pedal
Front: right-hand lever. Rear: right-foot pedal
Front and rear: one shared right-foot pedal
explanation: Most motorcycles have two brake controls: you squeeze the front brake lever on the right handgrip and press the rear brake pedal with your right foot.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (Motorcycle Controls)

prompt: Which control is operated with the left hand on a motorcycle with a manual transmission?
choices: The clutch lever
The front brake lever
The throttle
The rear brake
explanation: The clutch lever is on the left handgrip. The right hand handles the throttle and front brake, and the left foot operates the gearshift.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 8 (Motorcycle Controls)

prompt: What is the primary source of information on how your motorcycle should be inspected and maintained?
choices: Your state driver handbook
Its owner's manual
The dealer's sales brochure
Advice from other experienced riders
explanation: The owner's manual is the primary source for how a motorcycle should be inspected and maintained, including the schedule for regular upkeep.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: How often should you do a T-CLOCS pre-ride inspection?
choices: Once a week
Once a month
Only before long trips
Before every ride
explanation: A pre-ride inspection takes only a few minutes and should be done before every ride.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: In the T-CLOCS inspection, what does the "O" stand for?
choices: Odometer and gauges
Operator's license and papers
Overall appearance
Oil and other fluids
explanation: T-CLOCS stands for Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and other fluids, Chassis, and Stands.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: When checking the brakes during a pre-ride inspection, what should you confirm?
choices: Each brake alone feels firm and holds the motorcycle
The brakes squeak slightly when they are applied
Each brake feels soft at first, then grabs suddenly
The brake lever can be pulled all the way to the handgrip
explanation: Try the front and rear brake controls one at a time. Each should feel firm and hold the motorcycle when fully applied.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: During your pre-ride check, what should the throttle do when you release it?
choices: Stay at the position where you left it
Return slowly to idle over a few seconds
Snap back to fully closed
Close only partway to keep the engine running
explanation: The throttle should snap back to fully closed when released. A sticking throttle is a serious hazard.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: How should each mirror be adjusted?
choices: To show as much of your own arm and shoulder as possible
To show both the lane behind you and the lane beside you
To show only the lane next to you, not the lane behind
Pointed down slightly so that you can see your rear tire
explanation: Adjust each mirror so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you. It may show the edge of your arm or shoulder, but the road behind and to the side is what matters. Do this before starting, not while riding.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: Your motorcycle starts and runs briefly, then stalls. You forgot to open the fuel valve. Why did it start at all?
choices: A closed fuel valve only affects high-speed riding
The engine cut-off switch released reserve fuel
The fuel pump bypasses a closed valve while idling
It ran on fuel left in the lines
explanation: With the fuel valve closed, a motorcycle may start using the fuel still in the lines, but it will stall once the lines are empty. Make sure the valve is open, if equipped, before starting out.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: According to the T-CLOCS section, how often should brake hydraulic fluid and coolant levels be checked?
choices: Once a year
Weekly
Only when a warning light comes on
Every 10,000 miles
explanation: Check the brake hydraulic fluid and coolant level (if equipped) weekly. Engine oil and transmission fluid levels are part of the regular pre-ride check.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 9 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: During the "Stands" part of a pre-ride inspection, what should you confirm about the side stand?
choices: It hangs slightly down so it can be lowered quickly
It can hold the motorcycle up with a passenger aboard
It moves smoothly and its spring holds it firmly up
It is loose enough to swing freely while you ride
explanation: Make sure the side stand operates smoothly and that the spring holds it tightly up. A center stand, if equipped, should be held firmly against the frame while moving.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 10 (Check Your Motorcycle)

prompt: According to the MSF T-CLOCS checklist, when should tire air pressure be checked?
choices: When the tires are cold
Right after a highway ride, while the tires are hot
Only when a tire looks low or soft to the eye
After riding at least 10 miles to warm the tires up
explanation: The T-CLOCS checklist says to check tire air pressure when cold and adjust it to the load you are carrying.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 55 (T-CLOCS Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist)

prompt: While checking the throttle, you turn the handlebars from side to side. What should happen to the engine speed?
choices: It should rise slightly when you turn the bars left
It should stay steady, with no revving at any position
It should drop to idle only when the bars reach full lock
It should rise a little each time the bars reach full lock
explanation: The T-CLOCS checklist says the throttle should move freely, snap closed, and cause no revving when the handlebars are turned.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 55 (T-CLOCS Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist)

prompt: What does the MSF manual advise about add-ons and modifications?
choices: Avoid any that make the motorcycle more difficult to handle safely
Add as many accessories as you like if they are bolted on securely
Modifications are fine as long as a dealer installs them
Wait to modify the motorcycle until after its first oil change
explanation: To keep your motorcycle from causing you trouble, avoid add-ons and modifications that make it more difficult to handle.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 7 (Know Your Motorcycle)

prompt: Your front wheel and handlebars suddenly start to shake from side to side. What does the manual list among the most common causes?
choices: Shifting gears just before entering a turn
Riding in the center third of the lane
Using both brakes for every normal stop
Unsuitable accessories or improper loading
explanation: Most wobbles can be traced to improper loading, unsuitable accessories or incorrect tire pressure. Lighten or reposition the load and make sure windshields and fairings are mounted properly.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 33 (Wobble)

prompt: In the T-CLOCS checklist, how should you check engine oil level?
choices: Cold, on the side stand, on any surface
With the engine running at a fast idle
Warm, on the center stand, on level ground
Right after adding fuel, on the side stand
explanation: The checklist says to check engine oil warm, on the center stand, on level ground, using the dipstick or sight glass. Coolant, by contrast, is checked only when cool.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 55 (T-CLOCS Pre-Ride Inspection Checklist)

prompt: What does the MSF manual say riding gloves should be made of?
choices: Thin cotton, for the best feel of the controls
Leather or a similar durable material
Fingerless knit, so your fingers stay free
Light rubber, to keep your hands dry
explanation: Gloves allow a better grip and help protect your hands. They should be made of leather or a similar durable material.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 7 (Clothing)

prompt: Why does the manual stress dressing warmly for cold-weather rides?
choices: A warm rider can safely ride faster on cold roads
Bulky clothing makes you more visible to drivers
You cannot control a motorcycle well if you are numb
Cold weather causes the throttle to stick open
explanation: You cannot control a motorcycle well if you are numb, and riding for long periods in the cold can cause severe chill and fatigue. A winter jacket should resist wind and fit snugly at the neck, wrists and waist.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 7 (Clothing)
